title: A Town You Can Walk Past Without Seeing
question: Why do people live in Matmata?
message: This video tells curious adults that Amazigh families farm Matmata's dry hills by catching its rare rain behind earth walls called jessour, and dig their homes into the soft loess as cool farm storehouses, and that the same rain brought many homes down in 1969, yet some families still keep a room below ground.
angle: People live in Matmata because its dry hills can be farmed by catching rare autumn rain behind earth dams (jessour) for olives, figs and dates, and because thick wind-laid loess lets families dig cool, hidden farmhouse-storehouses around open pits, despite water once fetched by camel, windowless rooms, and the same rain that in 1969 brought many homes down and moved families up to New Matmata, where some still keep a room below for the summer.
ghi_chu_khung: Bản viết lại 29/11/2026 (bản 22/11 lưu ở script.v2.json; bản đầu ở script.v1.json), theo danh-gia-kich-ban-2026-11-29.md và research bổ sung S10–S31. Lập luận 'mưa mới là chủ nhà', khác Coober Pedy (tập 2: mỏ opal, trốn nắng, khoét ngang đồi): ở đây trốn nắng chỉ là giả thuyết đúng một nửa (cảnh 4); lời giải là jessour giữ mưa và đất cho ô liu/vả/chà là, nhà hố là nhà kho của nông trại (cảnh 5–6, ~3:00–4:30); đất loess là cơ chế (cảnh 7); cú lật là chính mưa phá nhà năm 1969 (cảnh 9), New Matmata, người giữ phòng dưới hố cho mùa nóng (cảnh 10). KHUNG TẬP (khác tập 6 Kiruna và tập 7 Mawsynram): 7 chương (Kiruna 8); một chuyến đi duy nhất vào tháng 10, không nhảy mùa, không nhịp 'quay lại mùa hè'; chương thân mở bằng doan-sai-roi-lat với hai giả thuyết ngay chương 1 (Kiruna mở bằng phong-quy-mo, Mawsynram dự kiến so-sanh-doi-thuong, Uros thu-hong-hieu); lời giải là cú lật bằng thời tiết xảy ra với chính Wob (mưa giữa sa mạc), kể bằng phong-quy-mo từ một giọt mưa ra cả thung lũng; chương nghiêm (1969) ở HỒI ỨC, Wob đặt mũ xuống ở mép một hố sập, không về bàn giữa tập (Kiruna về bàn); không chương nào đặt tên dạng 'Why…?', chương cuối đặt theo hành động vá vách chứ không theo 'kỷ vật quyết định'; outro ở bàn bằng khay cát và hai thìa nước (Kiruna: bật/tắt đèn bàn; Tristan: đọc bưu thiếp); đuôi mở bằng hành động đặt mẩu vách lên đĩa (không dùng 'X goes on the shelf' hay 'Up on the shelf, X gets'). So sánh đời thường: bưu điện chậm (c4), phễu và bọt biển (c5), đường nâu nén (c7), hũ bánh quy trên nóc tủ lạnh (c8); không mở bằng 'Think of…' hay 'Picture…'. Câu đối xứng 'not X, it's Y': 0 lần (c6 viết 'I'd been thinking of these pits as hiding places. They're farmhouses too.' để không mâu thuẫn với lý do ẩn mình ở c3) Nhóm 'here's…': 0 lần. CHUỖI ĐỒ VẬT WOB ĐỔI Ý: túi du lịch to. Cảnh 2: xếp đồ vào túi, cố ý không mang ô (định chuyển tới) → cảnh 4: dỡ hết đồ vào hốc tường phòng hố, gấp cả túi nhét vào (đổi ý 1: ở luôn) → cảnh 8: sau leo kho trượt, xách nước, phòng không cửa sổ, lặng lẽ xếp lại túi, để cạnh cửa (đổi ý 2) → cảnh 11: sau 'The house was here first', mở khoá túi lần nữa, đặt mũ lại vào hốc (đổi ý 3) → outro: WOULD MOVE, xô vữa cạnh giường. Chiếc ô: cảnh 2 bị đẩy vào góc; cảnh 5 Wob dùng mũ rộng vành thay ô, mũ đầy nước. Mũ: cảnh 9 đặt xuống đất (nghiêm), nhặt lên cuối cảnh; cảnh 10 đội lại. TRANG PHỤC WOB: trong chuyến đi: mũ rộng vành màu cát, khăn quàng mỏng, ba lô to, kéo túi du lịch to (cảnh 5 ướt sũng; cảnh 9 không đội mũ, mũ dưới đất). Ở bàn (cảnh 1, 2, 12, 13): đồ ở nhà, không ba lô, không mũ. ĐẠO CỤ XUYÊN TẬP: mẩu vách (1, 7, 12, 13); khay cát có lỗ tròn (2 → 12); đám mây 'ông chủ nhà' (6, 11, 12); thìa (12 hai thìa nước; cảnh 7 Wob chỉ hắt hơi, không cạo vách: Wob không phá nhà người ta); con dê (3, 8). Ảnh AI: không dùng (anh_ai rỗng); shots chỉ trỏ 2 bản đồ code (map-matmata, map-matmata-local) + thẻ chữ, mọi cảnh vẽ theo y_hinh. Người thật (bà Theouibi, bà Mohamedi, người thợ đào, Bourguiba) không vẽ mặt: người que, đồ vật hoặc thẻ chữ. Phim: chỉ nói tên phim và năm bằng lời; không vẽ nhân vật, đạo cụ, cảnh phim (y_hinh cảnh 11). Khách sạn Wob ở trong chuyến đi KHÔNG nêu tên (tránh ngụ ý một khách sạn có thật bị rơi vách).

scenes.narration: The town is Matmata, in the dry hills of southern Tunisia, about three hundred and sixty-five kilometres south of Tunis. That's around two hundred and twenty-five miles. From the road, I couldn't see a single house. I went to find out who would choose to live like that, and whether I could. I even packed to stay. A sun hat, sunscreen, and a very big bag. No umbrella. Why would I need one? By the end of the trip, I knew who really runs the place. It wasn't me. It wasn't the sun either. Somewhere in this story, a camel makes a delivery through a roof. I'll show you on a tray of sand.

scenes.narration: I arrived in October. I got out of the car in old Matmata and looked for the village. No rooftops. No walls. No windows. Just pale yellow hills, with round holes in them. My first guess was that everybody had left. A ghost town, with very tidy holes. Then a goat complained. Below me. I walked to the edge of the nearest hole and looked down. A courtyard, swept clean, with arched doorways cut into its walls, and washing on a line. The village hadn't left. The village was downstairs. I had walked straight over somebody's kitchen. Amazigh families, also called Berbers, have lived in homes like this for centuries. According to researchers who study these homes, the hills went through long stretches of raids and feuds. A house nobody can see is a hard house to rob.

scenes.narration: My second guess, I was sure of. They dug down to hide from the sun. I'd seen that trick before, on another trip. And I was half right. Researchers measured one of these rooms on a July day in nineteen ninety-seven. At three in the afternoon, the air outside hit forty-six degrees Celsius. That's about a hundred and fifteen Fahrenheit. Inside, the room sat at twenty-seven or twenty-eight all day. The ground is a very slow postal service. Summer heat takes about three months to reach ten metres down, about thirty-three feet. By the time it gets there, summer is long gone. I lay on my cool bed and unpacked my whole bag into a niche in the wall. I was moving in. I even wrote my new address on a postcard. Third hole on the left. Then a small question kept me awake. Plenty of places are hot. Why dig here, in these hills, and not somewhere easier?

scenes.narration: On my third day, it rained. In the desert. I had packed sunscreen. I stood under my sun hat while it filled up like a bowl, and I felt personally betrayed. The goat from my first day watched me from a dry doorway. These hills only get about two hundred millimetres of rain a year. That's around eight inches, and it comes in heavy, unpredictable bursts. So I followed the water. It ran off the bare hilltop into a narrow gully, and stopped against a wall of earth built straight across it. Behind the wall, a pool of muddy water. Above that, another wall, and another, like steps up the valley. On every step, trees. Olives, figs, date palms. These walls are called jessour. Each one catches the rain and the soil it carries, and holds them for the trees. Some stand taller than five metres, raised a little after every flood. The gully is a funnel. The jessour are the sponge at the bottom. With them, trees grow here that the rainfall alone could never support.

scenes.narration: Which brings me back to my pillow. How do you dig a house that doesn't fall on you? Mostly. The valleys here are filled with loess, fine dust laid down by the wind and packed hard. In places the layer is ten to twenty metres thick. You can dig it with a farm hoe, yet it stands up in straight walls on its own. It behaves a lot like packed brown sugar. Easy to carve. Holds its shape. Not a fan of water. So a family digs a deep, round courtyard, then carves rooms sideways into its walls. Almost nothing has to be built. No bricks. No beams. Just a lot of digging, and somewhere to put the dirt. I asked for a taller ceiling. Researchers who study these homes describe a rule of thumb. A room should never be bigger than the layer of earth left above it. My room had a curved ceiling. They're never flat here. I looked up at it and sneezed. The ceiling answered with a little dust, straight onto my pillow.

Like a cookie jar on top of the fridge, the point was to make it hard to reach. It was. I got a couple of footholds up and slid back down, gently, on my face. Animals and farm tools lived in niches along the entrance tunnel, away from the bedrooms. Then I tried the hardest job, which was water. scenes.narration: I set my hat down for this part. In the autumn of nineteen sixty-nine, rain fell across Tunisia for weeks. In early October, the coast below these hills got one hundred to two hundred millimetres in about six days. Up to a whole year's rain for Matmata, in less than a week. By the end of November, more than five hundred people had died in Tunisia, and more than seventy thousand homes had collapsed. Around Matmata, water poured into the pits, and many of these houses fell in. Families were offered land in a new town, New Matmata, for three dinars a square metre. The government of President Habib Bourguiba was building new towns above ground across the country, and many families moved into them. Some of the empty pit houses slowly fell into ruin. The rain that kept the trees alive had brought the walls down.

scenes.narration: The next morning I drove up to New Matmata. It's a short drive. One main road, cafés, a butcher, houses with windows. In my notebook I drew the trip as a dotted line, from the holes to the roofs. Then I learned the line runs both ways. Some people who moved into built houses, researchers found, kept a few rooms in their family's old pit house, for the long heat waves of summer. On a typical summer day, a built house measured over thirty-six degrees, and a pit room about twenty-five and a half. In winter, the pit room was the warmer one too. So some families commute between two homes. The commute is measured in degrees. I tried it myself. Lunch up top, at a café. Then a nap downstairs, in the cool, with my hat over my face.

scenes.narration: Back in the old town, I visited the most famous hole of all. In nineteen sixty-nine, a family home there became the Hotel Sidi Driss. In nineteen seventy-six, a film crew used it as a location for the first Star Wars film. Lucasfilm says a rare storm hit southern Tunisia soon after filming began there, and threw the schedule off. So even the film crew answered to the rain. Fans still come to stand in that courtyard. Around the town, Reuters found a few families still living underground in twenty eighteen, letting visitors look around for tips. One woman said leaving her house would be like throwing away her life and her traditions. The same reporters met a man who still knows how to dig these homes. His last new one was in the nineteen seventies. The visitors came for a film. The house was here first. Back in my room, the bag was still packed. I unzipped it again.

scenes.narration: The tray of sand on my desk still has its hole. I poured in one spoonful of water. The walls held. I poured in a second, and one side slumped. That's Matmata, explained by a spoon. People farm these hills because the rare rain can be caught, and they live inside them because the ground allows it. The price is that the rain gets a say. That same digger said he comes back to repair the houses every time it rains. I'd want him on speed dial. WOULD MOVE. I'd carry the water properly this time, help mend the walls every autumn, and keep a bucket of plaster by the bed, since I wobble into things. If you like quiet, cool rooms and don't miss windows, you'd settle in faster than me. I pressed the piece from my pillow into the slumped wall. It fits. It still drops a little dust, like it's thinking it over. Would you rather fight the heat every summer, or fix your walls after every rain?

verdict.label: WOULD MOVE

claims.quote: The town is Matmata, in the dry hills of southern Tunisia, about three hundred and sixty-five kilometres south of Tunis. That's around two hundred and twenty-five miles.
claims.statement: Matmata is a town in the dry hills of southern Tunisia (Gabès governorate), about 365 km (about 227 miles) south of the capital, Tunis.

claims.quote: No rooftops. No walls. No windows. Just pale yellow hills, with round holes in them.
claims.statement: Seen from ground level, traditional (old) Matmata shows almost no buildings: the homes are dug below ground around round pits, so the landscape appears as pale yellowish hills pocked with holes (a 'cratered landscape').

claims.quote: A courtyard, swept clean, with arched doorways cut into its walls
claims.statement: A traditional Matmata home is built around a sunken open courtyard pit, with rooms entered through arched doorways carved into the pit walls.

claims.quote: Amazigh families, also called Berbers, have lived in homes like this for centuries.
claims.statement: Amazigh (Berber) families in the Matmata area of southern Tunisia have lived in underground pit homes for centuries.

claims.quote: According to researchers who study these homes, the hills went through long stretches of raids and feuds. A house nobody can see is a hard house to rob.
claims.statement: Researchers studying the pit dwellings of south-eastern Tunisia link their hidden design (hard to see from a distance, indirect entrances, storerooms set high) to long periods of insecurity in these mountain villages, including raids and conflicts between tribes.

claims.quote: Researchers measured one of these rooms on a July day in nineteen ninety-seven. At three in the afternoon, the air outside hit forty-six degrees Celsius. That's about a hundred and fifteen Fahrenheit. Inside, the room sat at twenty-seven or twenty-eight all day.
claims.statement: In measurements on 24–25 July 1997 at a Matmata pit dwelling, the outdoor air temperature reached about 46 °C (about 115 °F) at 3 pm, while the room stayed at about 27–28 °C throughout the 24 hours.

claims.quote: Summer heat takes about three months to reach ten metres down, about thirty-three feet. By the time it gets there, summer is long gone.
claims.statement: At a depth of about 10 m (about 33 feet) the ground temperature around Matmata's pit dwellings is nearly constant, and the seasonal summer heat takes months to reach that depth, arriving long after summer has ended.

claims.quote: These hills only get about two hundred millimetres of rain a year. That's around eight inches, and it comes in heavy, unpredictable bursts.
claims.statement: The Matmata hills, where the pit-house villages are, receive on average about 200 mm (about 8 inches) of rain per year, and the rainfall is intense and irregular.

claims.quote: On every step, trees. Olives, figs, date palms. These walls are called jessour. Each one catches the rain and the soil it carries, and holds them for the trees.
claims.statement: In southern Tunisia's mountains, jessour are earth dams built across valleys and gullies that trap runoff water and the sediment it carries, creating terraced plots where olives, figs, date palms and other crops are grown.

claims.quote: Some stand taller than five metres, raised a little after every flood.
claims.statement: The earth dams (tabias) of the jessour system can be more than 5 m high and are progressively raised as each flood deposits more sediment behind them.

claims.quote: With them, trees grow here that the rainfall alone could never support.
claims.statement: By concentrating runoff, the jessour system allows crops such as olive trees to grow in southern Tunisia beyond the limits that local rainfall alone would allow.

claims.quote: The olive store sits high in the courtyard wall, half a floor or more above the ground. Its roof has an opening, and up top, the roof is just the hill. So olives could arrive by camel and be poured straight down into the store, without crossing the courtyard.
claims.statement: In the pit houses of south-eastern Tunisia, olive and grain storerooms are set half a storey to a full storey above the courtyard floor; olive stores have an opening in the roof, at ground level above, so olives brought by camel could be poured directly into the store without passing through the courtyard.

claims.quote: Under the courtyard sits a cistern. It catches the rain that falls into the yard.
claims.statement: In Matmata pit dwellings, a cistern beneath or within the courtyard collects the rainwater that falls into the courtyard.

claims.quote: Bread was baked down here. Grain was ground. Figs were dried in the sun.
claims.statement: In the pit houses of south-eastern Tunisia, the courtyard was used for household work such as making bread, grinding grain and drying figs.

claims.quote: The valleys here are filled with loess, fine dust laid down by the wind and packed hard. In places the layer is ten to twenty metres thick. You can dig it with a farm hoe, yet it stands up in straight walls on its own.
claims.statement: Valleys in the Matmata mountains are filled with loess (compacted fine wind-blown dust), 10–20 m thick, which can be dug with simple farm tools such as a hoe yet stands in vertical walls without collapsing.

claims.quote: So a family digs a deep, round courtyard, then carves rooms sideways into its walls. Almost nothing has to be built.
claims.statement: A Matmata pit dwelling consists of a deep, round courtyard pit with rooms excavated laterally into its walls, requiring almost no building materials.

claims.quote: Researchers who study these homes describe a rule of thumb. A room should never be bigger than the layer of earth left above it. My room had a curved ceiling. They're never flat here.
claims.statement: Researchers studying Matmata-area pit dwellings describe a rule of thumb for stability: a room's void should be smaller than the thickness of earth left above it; room ceilings are vaulted (curved), not flat.

claims.quote: Grain and olives were stored up high, reached by footholds cut into the wall, or by pegs of olive wood. Like a cookie jar on top of the fridge, the point was to make it hard to reach.
claims.statement: In pit houses of south-eastern Tunisia, grain and olive stores were set high in the courtyard walls and reached by footholds cut into the wall or olive-wood pegs driven into it, partly to protect stores against theft.

claims.quote: Animals and farm tools lived in niches along the entrance tunnel, away from the bedrooms.
claims.statement: In pit houses of south-eastern Tunisia, livestock stalls and storage for farm tools were placed in niches along the entrance tunnel, away from the living rooms, for hygiene.

claims.quote: A woman who used to live in one of these homes told the Associated Press about it. She remembered fetching water by camel from a distant spring, and searching for food every day.
claims.statement: In 2018, a woman who used to live in a traditional pit home in Matmata (Mahboub Theouibi, whose family later moved to a modern house) told the Associated Press she remembered fetching water by camel from a distant spring and searching for food every day.

claims.quote: My room got all its daylight from the courtyard.
claims.statement: Rooms in Matmata pit dwellings get their daylight mainly from the central courtyard.

claims.quote: In the autumn of nineteen sixty-nine, rain fell across Tunisia for weeks. In early October, the coast below these hills got one hundred to two hundred millimetres in about six days. Up to a whole year's rain for Matmata, in less than a week.
claims.statement: In autumn 1969 Tunisia had exceptional rain over about 40 days (September–October); during 3–8 October 1969 the south-eastern coastal area (Sfax, Gabès, Djerba) received 100–200 mm, comparable to the roughly 200 mm the Matmata hills receive in an average year.

claims.quote: By the end of November, more than five hundred people had died in Tunisia, and more than seventy thousand homes had collapsed.
claims.statement: By 27 November 1969, the 1969 floods in Tunisia had caused 542 deaths and the collapse of 70,540 houses, according to figures compiled in a UNESCO report (Pias 1970) cited by Boudhraâ and Cudennec.

claims.quote: Around Matmata, water poured into the pits, and many of these houses fell in. Families were offered land in a new town, New Matmata, for three dinars a square metre.
claims.statement: In 1969 flooding caused many cave and pit homes around Matmata to collapse, and displaced residents were sold land in New Matmata for 3 dinars per square metre, according to National Geographic.

claims.quote: The government of President Habib Bourguiba was building new towns above ground across the country, and many families moved into them.
claims.statement: Many families left Tunisia's underground homes when new towns and villages were built in the 1960s and 1970s under President Habib Bourguiba's modernisation drive.

claims.quote: Some of the empty pit houses slowly fell into ruin.
claims.statement: Many pit houses abandoned in the Matmata area gradually fell into ruin.

claims.quote: The next morning I drove up to New Matmata. It's a short drive. One main road, cafés, a butcher, houses with windows.
claims.statement: New Matmata, a short drive from old Matmata (about 14 km in a straight line), is a town of conventional above-ground houses with a main road, cafés and a butcher's shop.

claims.quote: Some people who moved into built houses, researchers found, kept a few rooms in their family's old pit house, for the long heat waves of summer.
claims.statement: Researchers report that some Matmata-area residents who moved to conventional houses have kept a few rooms in their ancestral pit dwellings to use during long summer heat waves.

claims.quote: On a typical summer day, a built house measured over thirty-six degrees, and a pit room about twenty-five and a half. In winter, the pit room was the warmer one too. So some families commute between two homes. The commute is measured in degrees.
claims.statement: Measurements compared by Krarti (1998) for a typical summer day in the Matmata area found a conventional built house above 36 °C indoors versus about 25.5 °C in a pit dwelling; on a typical winter day the pit dwelling was warmer (about 15 °C versus 10.5 °C).

claims.quote: In nineteen sixty-nine, a family home there became the Hotel Sidi Driss.
claims.statement: The Hotel Sidi Driss in Matmata was a traditional family home before it became a hotel in 1969.

claims.quote: In nineteen seventy-six, a film crew used it as a location for the first Star Wars film.
claims.statement: The Hotel Sidi Driss in Matmata was used in 1976 as a filming location for the first Star Wars film (A New Hope), whose Tunisian shoot began on 22 March 1976.

claims.quote: Lucasfilm says a rare storm hit southern Tunisia soon after filming began there, and threw the schedule off.
claims.statement: According to Lucasfilm (StarWars.com), soon after filming of the first Star Wars film began in Tunisia in March 1976, a rare storm hit southern Tunisia and disrupted the shooting schedule.

claims.quote: Fans still come to stand in that courtyard.
claims.statement: Star Wars fans still visit the Hotel Sidi Driss in Matmata to see the courtyard used in the film (AP reporting, 2018).

claims.quote: Around the town, Reuters found a few families still living underground in twenty eighteen, letting visitors look around for tips. One woman said leaving her house would be like throwing away her life and her traditions.
claims.statement: Reuters reported in February 2018 that a few families still live in underground pit houses around Matmata and let tourists visit in return for tips; one resident said leaving her house would be like throwing away her life and her traditions.

claims.quote: The same reporters met a man who still knows how to dig these homes. His last new one was in the nineteen seventies.
claims.statement: Reuters reported in 2018 that a man in the Matmata area who still knows how to dig traditional underground houses built his last new one in the 1970s.

claims.quote: People farm these hills because the rare rain can be caught, and they live inside them because the ground allows it.
claims.statement: Farming in the Matmata hills depends on capturing scarce runoff with jessour earth dams, and the area's thick, self-supporting loess allows dwellings to be excavated directly into the ground.

claims.quote: That same digger said he comes back to repair the houses every time it rains.
claims.statement: A man who still knows how to dig traditional underground houses in the Matmata area told Reuters in 2018 that he returns to repair them every time it rains, because heavy rain can make the earthen houses collapse.
